name: MinIO
summary: An S3-compatible object storage server that distributes object data across erasure-coded sets and repairs missing or damaged fragments through healing operations.

features.name: S3 object namespace
features.description: MinIO exposes bucket and object operations through an S3-compatible API, presenting a key-based object namespace above its storage implementation.
benefits: Allows clients and tools built for the S3 protocol to use the service
Separates object naming and API semantics from physical disk layout
costs: Object semantics do not provide relational querying or arbitrary in-place record updates
API compatibility still leaves deployment-specific consistency and feature behavior to verify

features.name: Erasure-coded object layout
features.description: The distributed server implementation organizes object data and parity across erasure sets, allowing an object to be reconstructed from surviving fragments subject to the configured quorum.
benefits: Uses parity to tolerate selected drive or node failures without simple full replicas
Makes storage protection a property of the distributed object layout
costs: Parity consumes capacity and adds encoding, decoding, and quorum work
Placement and failure domains constrain which failures can be tolerated

features.name: Background healing
features.description: MinIO includes healing operations that scan and repair missing or stale object and disk state after failures or topology changes.
benefits: Restores redundancy after a recoverable failure
Moves repair work into an explicit recovery mechanism instead of requiring manual object reconstruction
costs: Healing consumes disk, network, and CPU resources alongside foreground requests
Repair progress and remaining risk must be monitored during degraded operation

mathematical_views.question: How can a logical object key map to data and parity fragments distributed over a storage set while preserving reconstructability?
assumptions: The erasure-code parameters and placement set are fixed for the modeled write
The surviving fragment count meets the implementation's read or write quorum
Network, disk latency, and bit-level encoding costs are abstracted

mathematical_views.model: Repair transition system over fragment states
mathematical_views.question: How does an object move from degraded fragment state back to a redundant state after a disk or node failure?
assumptions: The object remains readable or reconstructable from surviving fragments
Healing can identify the missing or stale state and reach the affected storage endpoint
The model treats healing as a recovery transition and does not claim instantaneous durability

benefits: Broad client interoperability through an established object API
costs: Object-oriented access is a poor fit for transactional relational workloads

benefits: Failure tolerance with less redundancy than full replication in some layouts
costs: Parity and quorum operations reduce usable capacity and add failure-domain constraints

benefits: Restores redundancy without rebuilding the entire service manually
costs: Recovery competes with foreground workloads and extends degraded-state exposure
